routes.comment: The masthead mark. Beside styles.css because it is the same kind of thing: every page carries it, including the ones a signed-out visitor is meant to see, and the catch-all below would otherwise turn it into a 401 rewritten to the sign-in page.
The claim page is reached by someone with no account at all, following a link out of an email. It must render before there is any session to check.
The invitation page is reached the same way the claim page is -- out of an email, by somebody who may have no account. Same anonymous treatment, for the same reason.
Managing an archive's audience. Authenticated, and the API refuses anyone who is not an owner of the named slug -- this rule only decides who may load the markup.
Naming an archive and recording when it ends. Same treatment as /people/* and for the same reason: this rule decides who may load the markup, and the API decides who may change anything.
Making a hardcover of an archive. Same treatment again: the markup is served to anyone signed in and the API refuses anyone who is not an owner of the named slug.

Operator tooling: archives that have been deleted and not yet erased. `authenticated` is all this rule can say -- Static Web Apps roles are not where OPERATOR_EMAILS lives -- so the markup is served to any signed-in visitor and the API behind it returns 404 to everyone else. The page therefore renders nothing at all until that API confirms the caller, because an earlier version showed every signed-in visitor the heading, the explanation, and a promise that nobody else could see it. What remains is that a signed-in stranger can still read manage.html and manage.js as files; closing that needs a custom roles provider, not a route rule. Nothing links here.

Stopping our mail. Anonymous and it has to be: the person using it has never signed in and is not going to, and requiring an account would make the opt-out technically available and practically impossible.

How often we email somebody about new letters. Deliberately not under /settings: that route takes a slug and belongs to an archive's owner, while this one takes no slug at all and its audience is readers, who cannot open a slug's settings. A rewrite rule is required even though `/*` already covers the role, because navigationFallback would otherwise serve site.html and this is not an archive.

Asking a missionary to send the first letter. Anonymous for the same reason the opt-out is: the family member holding this link has never signed in, and this is the route out for the ones whose mail client cannot produce a forward we can verify.

Help pages, read by people with no account and often before they have decided whether to have one. Anonymous for the same reason the front page is: `/*` below is authenticated, so anything omitted here disappears behind a sign-in.
The sign-in chooser is anonymous and shows a provider icon, so the icon font has to be reachable without a session. It carries no archive data.

Describing a claim changes nothing and has to answer someone who has not signed in yet -- that is the whole point of the page. It must precede the /api/* rule, which matches first-wins. Redemption is deliberately not listed, so it falls through to authenticated.

Asking for a fresh claim link, offered on the page that says the old one is dead. Anonymous for the same reason describe is -- its entire audience is somebody who cannot sign in yet. The dead token in the body is the credential, and the reply never names an address, so it can ask that somebody be written to and cannot be used to learn who.
Same as claim/describe: the invitation page has to say who invited whom before anybody signs in. Accepting is not listed, so it falls through to authenticated.

Both halves of the opt-out are anonymous, unlike claim and invite where only the describe half is. There is no signed-in state to fall back on here: the whole point is that somebody who has never had an account can make the mail stop. Safe because the address to suppress is inside the token's signature rather than in the request -- the endpoint never takes anybody's word for whom to silence.
POST only, so no link-fetching scanner can spend it. This is also what a mail provider's one-click Unsubscribe posts to, per RFC 8058.

Both halves anonymous, like the opt-out and for the same reason: there is no signed-in state to fall back on, because the person using this has no account. Safe because both addresses -- who is written to, and on whose behalf -- are inside the token's signature rather than in the request.
POST only, and this one matters more than most: it sends mail to a missionary, and a GET would be spent by the first link scanner to open the message.

The print file, fetched by the printer rather than by a person. GET only, which is what separates it from the POST on the same prefix that asks for a checkout page -- that one is an owner pressing a button and falls through to authenticated below. Anonymous is not a relaxation here: the caller is a print facility that will never have an account, and the whole authorisation is a signature over the site and the book inside the token.

Peecho telling us an order was placed or changed. Anonymous for the same reason the print fetch is, and authorised the same way -- their SHA-256 of the secret key and the order id, checked before the body is believed. An allowlist of their addresses would be the alternative and would break the first time they moved a region.

globalHeaders.Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; img-src 'self' data:; style-src 'self'; script-src 'self'; object-src 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none'; base-uri 'none'; form-action 'self'
